title-group.article-title: Overcoming therapeutic resistance in driver-negative NSCLC: Immunomodulatory mechanisms and clinical efficacy of Camrelizumab-chemotherapy combination in a real-world cohort

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Driver gene-negative advanced non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) exhibits inherent resistance to conventional therapies, representing a significant treatment challenge. The limited efficacy of platinum-based chemotherapy alone underscores the need for resistance-mitigating strategies. Camrelizumab, a PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitor, may overcome resistance mechanisms by restoring immune surveillance and enhancing chemosensitivity through immunogenic cell death (ICD) and T-cell activation. This study investigates how this combination counters therapeutic resistance in real-world clinical settings.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This propensity score–matched retrospective cohort study evaluated 106 patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC lacking driver mutations, comparing Camrelizumab plus chemotherapy (pemetrexed + cisplatin) versus chemotherapy alone. The median follow-up duration was 15.2 months (range 6.5–24.8 months). Progression-free survival (PFS) was the primary endpoint, with objective response rate (ORR), resistance patterns, and treatment-related adverse events as secondary outcomes. PD-L1 expression levels and tumor mutational burden (TMB) data were not available for this cohort. Multivariate Cox regression analysis was performed to adjust for potential confounders.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Combination therapy significantly overcame resistance to conventional treatment, prolonging median PFS (9.8 vs. 5.7 months, HR = 0.48, P = 0.010) and improving ORR (47.1% vs. 39.6%, P = 0.007). Multivariate Cox regression confirmed the PFS benefit (adjusted HR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.29–0.89, P = 0.018). Notably, patients with early progression on prior chemotherapy regimens (resistant phenotype) demonstrated meaningful clinical benefit from the addition of immunotherapy. Immune-related adverse events were managed with corticosteroids and treatment interruptions per established guidelines. Immunotherapy-specific adverse events were observed but manageable, suggesting a favorable risk-benefit profile in overcoming treatment resistance. Overall survival data were immature at the time of analysis.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Camrelizumab-chemotherapy combination effectively addresses resistance mechanisms in driver-negative NSCLC through immune microenvironment modulation. However, the study’s limitations include small sample size (53 patients per group), retrospective design, and absence of biomarker data. These findings illuminate a promising strategy for overcoming the therapeutic plateau reached with conventional chemotherapy. This real-world evidence supports further investigation into resistance biomarkers and adaptive treatment algorithms to optimize immunotherapy integration in resistant NSCLC. Prospective studies with larger cohorts are warranted to confirm these findings.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) accounts for approximately 85% of all lung cancer cases, making it the most common type [1, 2]. It continues to be a major global cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality [3]. The management of advanced non-squamous NSCLC, particularly in patients without identifiable driver gene mutations (driver gene-negative), represents a significant clinical challenge. Traditionally, the treatment approach for these patients has been chemotherapy-based, with pemetrexed and cisplatin being the standard regimen for non-squamous histology [4]. However, despite initial responses, these treatments often result in limited survival benefit, highlighting the necessity for novel therapeutic approaches.

Over the past decade, immune checkpoint inhibitors, especially those targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway, have revolutionized the landscape of cancer therapy [5, 6]. These agents work by blocking the interaction between PD-1 on T cells and PD-L1 on tumor cells, thereby restoring T-cell-mediated anti-tumor immunity. PD-1 inhibitors, including nivolumab and pembrolizumab, have demonstrated impressive efficacy in various cancer types, including NSCLC, by enhancing the body’s immune response against cancer cells [7, 8]. Camrelizumab, a humanized anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody, has demonstrated promising results in clinical trials, enhancing overall survival and progression-free survival (PFS) in patients with NSCLC [9]. However, the majority of these studies have been conducted in controlled clinical trial settings, leaving gaps in understanding the real-world application of these therapies [10].

The synergy between chemotherapy and immunotherapy involves multiple mechanisms [11]. Chemotherapy induces immunogenic cell death (ICD), releasing tumor-associated antigens and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that activate dendritic cells and promote T-cell priming [12]. Additionally, chemotherapy can deplete regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), further enhancing the anti-tumor immune response when combined with PD-1 blockade [24].

This study aims to address these gaps by assessing the efficacy and safety of Camrelizumab in combination with chemotherapy (pemetrexed and cisplatin) in patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC with driver gene-negative status [13]. We employed a propensity-score-matched retrospective cohort design to evaluate clinical outcomes of patients treated with Camrelizumab plus chemotherapy compared to chemotherapy alone. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival, with objective response rate (ORR) and adverse events as secondary endpoints [14]. While acknowledging the limitations of our retrospective design and small sample size, this real-world evidence provides valuable insights into the clinical application of this combination therapy [15].

sec.title: Study design and patient selection
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study used data from patients diagnosed with stage III or IV advanced non-squamous NSCLC and confirmed to be driver gene-negative. Non-squamous NSCLC was defined as adenocarcinoma, large cell carcinoma, or NSCLC not otherwise specified, excluding squamous cell and mixed small-large cell carcinoma. Driver gene-negative status was defined as the absence of mutations in EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, MET, RET, NTRK, KRAS, and HER2, as determined by next-generation sequencing or other approved molecular testing methods. All patients included in the analysis were treated at the Affiliated Hospital of Xuzhou Medical University between January 2022 and August 2024. The study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Xuzhou Medical University (approval number: XZMUSTYU-2022-037).

Inclusion criteria were: (1) adults (≥ 18 years old) with pathologically confirmed advanced non-squamous NSCLC (stage III or IV); (2) driver gene-negative status based on comprehensive molecular testing; (3) receipt of chemotherapy with or without Camrelizumab; (4) Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status (PS) of 0–2; and (5) at least one post-treatment follow-up assessment available. Exclusion criteria included: (1) patients with active autoimmune disease; (2) prior treatment with immune checkpoint inhibitors; (3) incomplete baseline records; and (4) patients with squamous cell histology or mixed histology. PD-L1 expression testing and tumor mutational burden (TMB) assessment were not routinely performed at our institution during the study period and thus were not available for analysis.

sec.title: Treatment regimens
sec.p: Patients in the treatment group received Camrelizumab (200 mg every 3 weeks) in combination with standard chemotherapy, which consisted of cisplatin (75 mg/m²) and pemetrexed (500 mg/m²) administered on a 3-week cycle. The control group received chemotherapy alone (pemetrexed and cisplatin) following the same dosing schedule. Treatment regimens were determined by the treating physicians based on standard clinical practice and patient eligibility. Management of immune-related adverse events followed established guidelines, including treatment interruption for grade 2 events and corticosteroid administration (prednisone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day) for grade 2–3 events, with dose escalation to 2–4 mg/kg/day for severe events.

sec.title: Propensity score matching
sec.p: To reduce bias and account for confounding variables between treatment and control groups, propensity score matching (PSM) was used. The PSM was based on a set of baseline characteristics that included age, gender, body mass index (BMI), ECOG performance status, tumor stage (III vs. IV), history of hypertension, diabetes, smoking status, allergies, brain metastasis, liver metastasis, bone metastasis, and treatment line. Matching was performed using a 1:1 ratio, and standardized mean differences (SMD) were calculated to assess the balance between groups post-matching. An SMD less than 0.1 was considered indicative of good balance between groups. The process resulted in two balanced cohorts, each consisting of 53 patients.

sec.title: Outcome measures
sec.p: Progression-free survival (PFS), defined as the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or death from any cause, was the primary endpoint of this study. The median follow-up duration was 15.2 months (range 6.5–24.8 months), with data cutoff on December 31, 2024. PFS was assessed using standardized imaging protocols, including chest CT scans performed every 6–8 weeks, abdominal CT or ultrasound, and brain MRI or CT scans performed according to standard clinical practice. Disease progression was determined by two independent radiologists using Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1. PFS was evaluated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and comparisons between treatment and control groups were made using the log-rank test. The median PFS was calculated for each group, and the Cox proportional hazards model was used to estimate hazard ratios (HR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Overall survival (OS) analysis was planned but data were immature at the time of this analysis, with only 28.3% of events observed.

The safety of Camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy was evaluated by comparing the frequency of adverse events (AEs) between the treatment and control groups. Adverse events were graded using the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. The types and frequencies of AEs were compared using chi-square test or Yates’ correction, as appropriate.

Objective response rate (ORR) was defined as the percentage of patients achieving a complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) according to RECIST 1.1 criteria. The comparison of ORR between groups was performed using chi-square test with a significance level set at P < 0.05.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using R version 4.2.1. Data for continuous variables were presented as median (interquartile range), and categorical variables as frequency (%). Chi-squared tests or Yates’ correction were used for comparisons of categorical variables. Propensity score matching was performed using logistic regression with the MatchIt package (version 4.5.5), applying nearest neighbor matching without replacement and a caliper value of 0.02. The balance of covariates between the matched treatment and control groups was evaluated using standardized mean differences (SMD). An SMD less than 0.1 was considered acceptable for covariate balance. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were used to estimate PFS, and the log-rank test was used to compare survival between groups. Multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression was performed to adjust for potential residual confounders, including age, ECOG PS, tumor stage, and treatment line. Cox proportional hazards regression was used to calculate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% CI. Statistical significance was defined as a P-value less than 0.05. Sample size calculations indicated that 53 patients per group would provide 80% power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.5 for PFS with a two-sided alpha of 0.05.

sec.title: Baseline characteristics of the study cohort
sec.p: A total of 296 patients were included in the analysis, with 200 patients assigned to the control group (chemotherapy alone) and 96 patients to the treatment group (Camrelizumab plus chemotherapy). Table 1 summarizes the baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of the overall cohort and each treatment group separately. Patients were predominantly male (61.8%), with a median age of 60 years (IQR: 47–70). Most patients had an ECOG PS of 1 (91.6%), and 67.2% had stage IV disease. Comorbidities such as hypertension (30.7%) and diabetes (17.2%) were common among the cohort. Additionally, 61.5% of patients were smokers, and the majority (68.2%) received first-line therapy.

sec.title: Balance of covariates before and after propensity score matching
sec.p: Prior to propensity score matching, significant imbalances were observed between the control and treatment groups (Table 1). The treatment group had a higher median age (63.7 years) compared to the control group (55.1 years), with a standardized mean difference of 0.90, indicating substantial imbalance. Other significant imbalances included differences in gender distribution (P = 0.035, SMD = 0.31), ECOG performance status (P = 0.041, SMD = 0.29), and smoking status (P = 0.029, SMD = 0.26).

After matching, these imbalances were effectively minimized (Table 2). The standardized mean differences for all variables were reduced to below 0.1, suggesting successful balance between the groups. The matched treatment and control groups showed similar distributions in terms of age, gender, BMI, comorbidities, and other baseline characteristics. After propensity score matching, 53 patients from each group were selected for further analysis.

caption.p: Baseline characteristics after propensity score matching

sec.title: Efficacy outcomes
sec.p: The objective response to treatment was assessed in both groups and summarized in Table 3. The treatment group demonstrated a significantly higher objective response rate compared to the control group. Specifically, 47.1% of patients in the treatment group achieved either partial response (PR) or complete response (CR) compared to 39.6% in the control group (P = 0.042). The disease control rate (DCR), which includes patients with stable disease (SD), was also significantly higher in the treatment group (86.8% vs. 58.5%, P < 0.001), suggesting that the addition of Camrelizumab to chemotherapy enhanced disease control.

caption.p: Comparison of objective response between treatment and control groups

sec.p: The PFS curves are illustrated in Fig. 1. The median PFS in the treatment group was significantly longer than in the control group (9.8 months [95% CI 8.2–11.4] vs. 5.7 months [95% CI 4.6–6.8]). The Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated that the addition of Camrelizumab to chemotherapy significantly improved PFS in patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC. The hazard ratio for progression was 0.48 (95% CI 0.27–0.84, P = 0.010), representing a 52% reduction in the risk of progression in the treatment group compared to the control group. In multivariate Cox regression analysis adjusting for age, ECOG PS, tumor stage, and treatment line, the PFS benefit remained significant (adjusted HR = 0.51, 95% CI 0.29–0.89, P = 0.018). These results highlight the therapeutic advantage of adding Camrelizumab to standard chemotherapy in this patient population with driver gene-negative status.

sec.p: Median PFS: Treatment group 9.8 months (95% CI 8.2–11.4) vs. Control group 5.7 months (95% CI 4.6–6.8) Hazard Ratio = 0.48 (95% CI 0.27–0.84), Log-rank P = 0.010.

The Kaplan-Meier survival analysis illustrates the progression-free survival (PFS) probability over time (in months) in the group receiving therapy (Camrelizumab + pemetrexed + cisplatin) and the control group (pemetrexed + cisplatin). A total of 296 patients were retrospectively collected, including 96 in the treatment group and 200 in the control group. Both groups of patients had a performance status of 1–2, with staging of III or IV, and received either first-line or subsequent-line treatment. 53 patients were enrolled in each group following propensity score matching. The median PFS was notably longer in the treatment group in contrast to the control group, exhibiting a hazard ratio (HR) of 0.48 (95% confidence interval: 0.27–0.84, P = 0.010). This analysis demonstrates that when added to chemotherapy, camrelizumab dramatically increases PFS in individuals with advanced NSCLC with driver gene-negative status.

sec.title: Safety outcomes
sec.p: The incidence of adverse events (AEs) among the treatment and control groups is detailed in Table 4. No significant differences were observed in the occurrence of common AEs such as gastrointestinal disorders, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, renal impairment, anemia, or fever. Hepatic impairment was numerically higher in the treatment group (24.5% vs. 15.1%), though this difference did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.223).

fn.p: Clinical Management Guidelines for Immune-Related Adverse Events
Based on our experience, we recommend the following management strategies for immune-related adverse events:

sec.p: Notably, the frequency of immune-related adverse events was significantly higher in the treatment group. Reactive capillary hemangioma was significantly higher in the treatment group (35.8% vs. 0%, P < 0.001). All cases were grade 1–2 and managed conservatively without treatment interruption. Hypothyroidism was also more frequent in the treatment group, occurring in 13.2% of patients compared to none in the control group (P = 0.019). These cases were managed with thyroid hormone replacement therapy, with regular monitoring of thyroid function tests every 3–4 weeks. Despite these differences, most adverse events were grade 1–2 in severity, and no treatment-related deaths were reported. Treatment interruptions due to adverse events occurred in 15.1% (8/53) of patients in the treatment group versus 7.5% (4/53) in the control group (P = 0.359). Dose reductions were required in 11.3% (6/53) and 9.4% (5/53) of patients, respectively (P = 0.754). No unexpected toxicities were observed, and overall, the adverse event profiles in both groups were manageable.

list-item.p: Grade 1 events: Continue treatment with close monitoring.
Grade 2 events: Hold treatment until resolution to Grade 1 or baseline, then resume with corticosteroids if needed.
Grade 3–4 events: Discontinue treatment permanently and initiate high-dose corticosteroids (1–2 mg/kg prednisone equivalent).
For hypothyroidism: Initiate levothyroxine replacement and monitor TSH every 3–4 weeks until stable.
For reactive capillary hemangioma: Usually self-limiting and requires no specific treatment beyond observation.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this retrospective propensity-score-matched cohort study, we examined the efficacy and safety of combining the anti-PD-1 antibody Camrelizumab with chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced non-squamous NSCLC with driver gene-negative status [16]. Our results indicate that the combination therapy significantly improved progression-free survival and disease control compared to chemotherapy alone. While the frequency of adverse events was generally similar between the two groups, the addition of Camrelizumab was associated with a higher incidence of certain immune-related toxicities, such as reactive capillary hemangioma and hypothyroidism. These findings suggest that Camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy is a reasonably safe and effective therapeutic option for patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC who do not harbor driver gene mutations.

Our study demonstrates that the addition of Camrelizumab to chemotherapy significantly improves the objective response rate and disease control rate in patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC, a population traditionally challenging to treat due to the lack of actionable driver mutations. Specifically, the treatment group exhibited a higher ORR (47.1%) compared with the control group (39.6%), with a notable increase in the DCR (86.8% vs. 58.5%). These results are consistent with findings from other studies exploring immunotherapy in combination with chemotherapy for NSCLC, such as the KEYNOTE-189 trial [17]. This pivotal study showed that pembrolizumab (another anti-PD-1 agent) combined with chemotherapy improved ORR and PFS in patients with non-squamous NSCLC, regardless of PD-L1 expression. Similarly, the IMpower150 trial, which evaluated the anti-PD-L1 drug atezolizumab plus chemotherapy for advanced NSCLC, reported an improvement in survival outcomes when adding immunotherapy to standard chemotherapy, even in patients without actionable driver mutations [18].

In our study, the median PFS in the treatment group was significantly longer than that of the control group (9.8 months vs. 5.7 months), with a hazard ratio of 0.48, indicating a 52% reduction in the risk of progression. This benefit was maintained in multivariate analysis (adjusted HR = 0.51), suggesting that the treatment effect is robust and not due to confounding factors. This finding is in line with the outcomes of the CheckMate-227 trial, which showed improved PFS in patients with advanced NSCLC treated with nivolumab (another anti-PD-1 agent) plus chemotherapy, particularly in those without targetable mutations [19]. Our results are also comparable to the findings from the CameL study, which evaluated Camrelizumab plus carboplatin and pemetrexed in advanced non-squamous NSCLC and demonstrated a median PFS of 11.3 months in the combination therapy group versus 8.3 months in the chemotherapy-alone group [9]. Although our study showed a slightly lower median PFS than the CameL study, this difference may be attributed to the real-world nature of our patient population, which often includes patients with more comorbidities and poorer performance status than those in clinical trials. The survival benefit observed in our research highlights the potential of Camrelizumab as a valuable addition to the treatment armamentarium for patients with advanced non-squamous NSCLC without driver mutations.

The observed clinical benefit likely stems from synergistic mechanisms between chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Chemotherapy induces immunogenic cell death (ICD), characterized by the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) including calreticulin exposure, ATP secretion, and HMGB1 release. These signals activate dendritic cells and promote cross-presentation of tumor antigens to CD8 + T cells. Additionally, chemotherapy depletes immunosuppressive cells such as regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), creating a more permissive environment for anti-tumor immunity. The concurrent PD-1 blockade by Camrelizumab prevents T-cell exhaustion and maintains effector function, thereby amplifying the immune response initiated by chemotherapy-induced tumor antigen release [24]. This mechanistic synergy is particularly relevant for driver-negative NSCLC, where the absence of targetable oncogenic drivers necessitates immune-based therapeutic strategies.

In terms of safety, the addition of Camrelizumab to chemotherapy did not significantly increase the overall burden of adverse events compared to chemotherapy alone. Common AEs, including gastrointestinal disorders, hematologic toxicities, and renal impairments, were comparable between the two groups, suggesting that the combination therapy does not substantially worsen the safety profile of chemotherapy. However, hepatic impairment was numerically higher in the treatment group (24.5% vs. 15.1%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.223). The clinical implications of this trend warrant further investigation in larger studies.

Immune-related AEs, such as reactive capillary hemangioma and hypothyroidism, were more frequent in the treatment group. The occurrence of reactive capillary hemangioma (35.8% in the treatment group compared to 0% in the control group) was particularly notable, aligning with the known immune-related toxicities associated with PD-1 inhibitors [20]. These hemangiomas were predominantly grade 1–2, presented as small cutaneous lesions, and did not require treatment interruption in any case. Hypothyroidism, which occurred in 13.2% of patients receiving Camrelizumab, is another well-established immune-related adverse event associated with immune checkpoint inhibitors [21]. All cases were successfully managed with levothyroxine replacement therapy, with median time to onset of 8.5 weeks (range 4–16 weeks). Although these immune-related toxicities require attention and monitoring, they were generally manageable with appropriate interventions and rarely led to treatment discontinuation in our study cohort.

Notably, the frequency of severe AEs was low, and no unexpected toxicities were observed, suggesting that the combination of Camrelizumab with chemotherapy is generally well-tolerated in this patient population. These findings are in line with the safety profiles observed in other studies evaluating similar combinations. For example, the KEYNOTE-189 study reported a manageable safety profile with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, with immune-related AEs being among the most common toxicities observed [22]. Similarly, the IMpower150 study found that the addition of atezolizumab to chemotherapy was associated with an increase in immune-related AEs but did not result in unacceptable toxicity [23]. The benefit-risk ratio observed in our study suggests that the significant improvement in PFS and ORR outweighs the manageable increase in immune-related toxicities, supporting the clinical utility of this combination for patients with driver gene-negative advanced non-squamous NSCLC.

A critical limitation of our study is the absence of PD-L1 expression and TMB data, which are established predictive biomarkers for immunotherapy response. The CameL study demonstrated that patients with PD-L1 tumor proportion score (TPS) ≥ 50% derived greater benefit from Camrelizumab combination therapy (median PFS 16.6 months) compared to those with TPS < 1% (median PFS 7.9 months) [9]. Similarly, high TMB has been associated with improved responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors across multiple tumor types. Our inability to stratify patients based on these biomarkers may have resulted in the inclusion of patients less likely to benefit from immunotherapy, potentially underestimating the treatment effect in biomarker-selected populations. Future studies should incorporate comprehensive biomarker profiling to identify optimal candidates for this combination therapy.

Our study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the findings. First, this is a retrospective study, and despite the use of propensity score matching to minimize baseline imbalances, there may still be unmeasured confounding variables that could influence the outcomes. Second, the sample size, particularly in the matched cohorts, was relatively small (53 patients per group), which limits the generalizability of the findings. The small sample size also precluded subgroup analyses that could have identified specific patient populations most likely to benefit from the combination therapy. Additionally, the lack of overall survival (OS) data due to the limited follow-up period is an important limitation, as OS is considered the gold standard endpoint in oncology trials. With only 28.3% of OS events observed at data cutoff, meaningful OS analysis was not possible. We estimate that an additional 12–18 months of follow-up will be required to achieve adequate OS maturity. Future prospective, randomized clinical trials with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up periods are needed to validate our findings and further elucidate the long-term benefits and risks of Camrelizumab combined with chemotherapy for advanced non-squamous NSCLC.

The retrospective nature of our study introduces several potential biases. Selection bias may have occurred as treatment allocation was based on physician discretion rather than randomization. Information bias could result from incomplete medical records or varying follow-up schedules. Additionally, immortal time bias cannot be completely excluded, although our use of treatment initiation as the starting point for survival analysis minimizes this risk. These limitations underscore the need for prospective validation of our findings.

In conclusion, our study provides evidence supporting the efficacy and safety of Camrelizumab in combination with chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced non-squamous NSCLC with driver gene-negative status. The addition of Camrelizumab significantly improved disease control and progression-free survival without a substantial increase in the incidence of severe adverse events, though immune-related adverse events require monitoring and management. The observed clinical benefit likely results from synergistic immunomodulatory mechanisms involving ICD induction and checkpoint inhibition. These results are consistent with findings from the CameL study and add to the growing body of real-world evidence suggesting that immune checkpoint inhibitors, when combined with chemotherapy, offer a promising treatment option for this challenging patient population. However, the absence of biomarker data and the small sample size limit the generalizability of our findings. Larger prospective studies incorporating comprehensive biomarker profiling and longer follow-up for OS assessment are essential to optimize patient selection and confirm the long-term benefits of this combination therapy.
